timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Sometimes in astronomy it's not what you see, but what you don't see that says the most.
That may be the case with 47 Tukane, a densely packed star cluster in the southern hemisphere.
Astronomer Ron Gilliland surveyed 47 Tuk looking for a certain class of planets, so called
hot Jupiters, because they're roughly the same size as Jupiters but live in very tight
orbits around their stars and are common in our part of the galaxy.
The eight day Hubble survey turned up a surprise, and 35,000 star surveyed no planets.
None.
Gilliland's team fine-tuned Hubble so that it could see the slide dimming of stars that
happens when a Jupiters-sized planet passes between them and the Earth.
In fact, the search technique was so sensitive that Hubble did pick up the variations in several
binary star pairs, but still no planets.
47 Tukane is very different from our local neighborhood.
Stars are much closer together, and they lack the heavy metals common in our area.
This result doesn't rule out the presence of other planets, but the zero score may have
a lot to say about some of astronomy's biggest questions.
I think that's telling us that it's probably the case that stars born into this environment.
Very crowded low-metalicity are not likely, not as likely, to have planets as those in
the local environment.
Astronomers need more data from 47 Tukane to determine whether the cluster's lack of metals
or its tidal forces or some other unknown force keeps the hot Jupiters from forming.
I think that's telling us that it's probably the case that stars born into this environment
are not likely, not as likely, to have planets as those in the local environment.

youtube_description: This videotape has seven segments, discussing and showing the evidence for the proposition that the galactic clusters do not have many planets. Specifically the segments show: (1) Dr. Ron Gilliland discussing the process of looking for "Hot Jupiters" (i.e., planets about the size of Jupiter, which are hotter than Jupiter) in the globular clusters, (2) a zoom into 47 Tucanae globular cluster, (3) an animation of a planet passing between the host star and the earth with a brightness graph, (4) the same animation as before without the graph, (5) Ron Gilliland of the Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI) discussing possible interpretations of his findings in the 47 Tucanae globular cluster, (6) Ron Gilliland examining the images of 47 Tucanae, and (7) images of 47 Tucanae watching for variations in brightness.
youtube_title: Astronomers Ponder Lack of Planets in Globular Cluster
